subsection: 10. Cultural revivals and the consolidation of Catholic identity

notes.h: Douglas Hyde and the de-anglicisation argument (1892)
notes.b: Hyde’s lecture of 1892 gave the cultural revival its programme: Irish people should reject English habits and revive their own language and customs.
points: Douglas Hyde delivered his lecture The Necessity for De-Anglicising Ireland to the National Literary Society in Dublin in November 1892.
Hyde argued that the English language, dress, customs and sports had replaced Irish culture among the people, and that the Irish should recover their own traditions.
Hyde did not reject the British connection itself, and he argued that de-anglicisation was compatible with loyalty to the Crown and with a strong Irish identity.
The lecture set the terms for the Gaelic League’s work and for the later debate on Irish Ireland.

notes.b: The Gaelic League, founded in 1893, set out to revive the Irish language through classes, publications and festivals.
points: The Gaelic League, Conradh na Gaeilge, was founded in Dublin on 31 July 1893 by Douglas Hyde and Eoin MacNeill.
The League ran Irish-language classes in towns and villages, and its teachers and organisers travelled widely to set them up.
The League held feiseanna, competitive festivals of Irish music, song and dance, which helped to make Irish culture a public activity.
An Claidheamh Soluis, the League’s weekly newspaper, was established in 1899 and carried news of its activities and debate on Irish politics.
The League’s campaigns achieved the inclusion of Irish in the primary school programme in 1900, and it promoted St Patrick’s Day as a national festival.
The League was non-political in its early rules, but its members included many nationalists, and its later politicisation was led by Patrick Pearse, who edited An Claidheamh Soluis from 1903 to 1909.

notes.b: Moran’s Irish Ireland movement argued that Catholic, Gaelic and rural values should define the nation, and it attacked Anglo-Irish cultural influence.
points: D.P. Moran, the editor of The Leader newspaper founded in 1900, popularised the phrase Irish Ireland to describe a Catholic and Gaelic national identity.
Moran argued that Irish nationalists should favour Irish goods, Irish language and Catholic morality, and he criticised the Anglo-Irish gentry and the Protestant middle class.
Moran’s book The Philosophy of Irish Ireland, published in 1905, set out his case for a self-sufficient Catholic and Gaelic nation.
The Irish Ireland movement drew on the Gaelic League and the GAA, but it also divided the revival between cultural and religious nationalists.

notes.b: Hyde was the Gaelic League’s founder and first president, and his scholarship and advocacy made him the most prominent figure of the language revival.
points: Douglas Hyde (1860–1949) was born in Co. Roscommon, the son of a Church of Ireland clergyman, and he learned Irish from native speakers in the west.
As a participant, Hyde founded the Gaelic League in 1893 and was its first president, and he collected Irish folk tales and songs that were published in English and Irish.
Contemporaries saw Hyde as a scholar and an advocate of the language, and many Protestant and Catholic cultural nationalists admired his non-sectarian approach.
Nationalists in the Irish Ireland movement criticised Hyde as too moderate, and his resignation from the League in 1915 followed disputes over its politicisation.
Historians judge Hyde as a central figure of the cultural revival, and he became the first President of Ireland in 1938.

notes.b: A group of writers led by Yeats and Lady Gregory created an Irish national theatre that drew on Irish myth and the speech of rural Ireland.
points: The Irish Literary Theatre was founded in 1899 by W.B. Yeats, Lady Gregory and Edward Martyn, to create a national drama in Ireland.
The Abbey Theatre opened in Dublin on 27 December 1904, with funding from Annie Horniman and support from the Irish National Theatre Society.
John Millington Synge’s The Playboy of the Western World caused riots in the Abbey Theatre in January 1907, as audiences objected to its portrayal of rural Ireland.
The Hugh Lane gallery dispute of the 1900s and 1910s concerned Lane’s offer of a collection of modern art to Dublin, which was tied to a dispute over where a gallery should be built.

notes.b: Yeats was the leading poet and dramatist of the Literary Revival, and his work combined Irish myth with a critique of Irish public life.
points: William Butler Yeats (1865–1939) was born in Dublin, the son of a painter, and he was educated partly in London and Sligo.
As a participant, Yeats founded the Irish Literary Theatre and was a director of the Abbey Theatre, and his plays, including Cathleen ni Houlihan, were staged there.
Contemporaries saw Yeats as an Anglo-Irish poet whose work was admired by nationalists but who was viewed with suspicion by Irish Ireland critics.
Yeats’s poem September 1913 responded to the Dublin lockout and criticised the commercial spirit of Dublin’s leading men.
Historians place Yeats at the centre of the revival, and his later career as a senator in the Free State and a Nobel Prize winner in 1923 is often noted.
Historians differ over Yeats’s politics: some see him as an aristocratic critic of mass nationalism, while others see him as a national poet who shaped Irish identity.

notes.h: Catholic identity: churches, schools and devotion
notes.b: The consolidation of Catholic identity drew on building, schooling and devotional organisations in the decades after 1870.
points: Catholic church building expanded across Ireland in the late nineteenth century, and many new churches were built in towns and villages.
The Catholic Church controlled most primary and secondary schools, and it used this control to shape religious education and to promote Catholic devotion.
St Patrick’s College, Maynooth trained priests for the Irish church, and its graduates held a respected position in rural communities.
Confraternities and sodalities organised Catholic devotion among men and women, and they were a central feature of parish life.
The Pioneer Total Abstinence Association was founded in 1898 by Fr James Cullen, a Jesuit, to promote abstinence from alcohol among Catholics.
The Ne Temere decree of 1908 required that children of mixed marriages be brought up as Catholics, and it caused controversy among Protestants.

notes.h: The GAA after 1891 and the Irish Republican Brotherhood
notes.b: The GAA recovered after 1891, and its links to the IRB made it part of the separatist culture of the revival.
points: The GAA recovered in the 1890s, and it reorganised its county boards and resumed the championships.
The IRB’s members became active in the GAA’s leadership, and the association was closely linked to separatist politics in the early twentieth century.
The GAA and the Gaelic League shared members and supporters, and their combined work made Irish games and language central to Irish identity.

notes.h: Assessment: the revival and Catholic identity
notes.b: Judgements on the cultural revival compare its contribution to Irish identity with its divisions between cultural and religious nationalism.
points: Achievement: the Gaelic League, the Literary Revival and the GAA created a lasting cultural identity, and the language and games became national symbols.
Limit: the revival’s Catholic and Gaelic emphasis alienated many Protestants and Anglo-Irish people, and the language itself declined in the Irish-speaking districts.
Contemporary unionists saw the revival as a threat to the Union, while nationalists saw it as the basis of a new Irish nation.
Historians see the revival as a cultural movement that shaped the nationalism of 1916 and the Free State, but they differ on how far Catholic identity and Irish Ireland shaped the Irish state.

keyTerms.definition: The adoption of English language, customs and culture in Ireland, which the revival sought to reverse.
The reversal of anglicisation through the revival of the Irish language, games and customs, as set out by Douglas Hyde in 1892.
The movement that defined the nation through Catholic, Gaelic and rural values, promoted by D.P. Moran.
The Protestant landed and professional class of Ireland with English cultural connections, whose writers helped to create the Literary Revival.
The Conradh na Gaeilge, founded in 1893 to revive the Irish language through classes, festivals and publications.
The movement of writers such as Yeats, Lady Gregory and Synge, which drew on Irish myth and rural speech to create a national literature and theatre.
The national theatre opened in Dublin in 1904, which staged the plays of the Literary Revival.
The 1908 Catholic decree on mixed marriages, which required children to be raised as Catholics.
